source.title: Why Do Speech Language Models Fail to Generate Semantically Coherent Outputs? A Modality Evolving Perspective
source.authors: Hankun Wang; Hao-Ran Wang; Yi-Wei Guo; Zhi-Han Li; Chenpeng Du; Xie Chen; Kai Yu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether downstream task accuracy changes predictably with training scale, using task accuracy versus processed-token checkpoints rather than the original studies' held-out loss measurements.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports accuracy across trained-token checkpoints for three objective tasks and six modality-specific models, so these results bear on V6. Table 3 and Table 4 compare modalities at convergence, and Figures 2–3 compare internal-layer outputs; they do not measure a scaling relationship named by the claim versions. Validation loss is used to determine convergence, but no loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute scaling result is reported.
record.test_reason: Section 5.2 follows Kaplan-style scaling. It plots zero-shot task accuracy against trained tokens on log-log axes for six 1.1B speech/phone/text LMs. The authors report that straight lines fit and slopes are positive, which bears on V6 in a new setting (speech and phone token LMs). No loss-versus-scale fits are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that paralinguistic variability (factor C) most impedes speech LMs, especially lexical modeling, and that longer sequences (factor B) hurt syntax and semantics. In Section 5.2 they also report that task accuracy scales log-linearly with trained tokens, with slower scaling for speech-like modalities. They draw no conclusion about loss scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a fixed 1.1B-parameter model and compares downstream task accuracy at checkpoints within the first training epoch; it does not fit held-out loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The trend is reported separately by modality and task; Speech-HuBERT on sWUGGY is the stated exception to positive slopes.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: For the scaling result, only one model size is used; checkpoints cover the first epoch; the measure is task accuracy rather than held-out loss; and Figure 1 provides no stated numeric slopes or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant scaling rows left out. Tables 3–4 report converged modality comparisons, while Figures 2–3 report layer-wise task accuracy; these do not measure the scaling relationships in the claim versions.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; a single model size is used.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Speech-modality loss power laws are not measured; only downstream accuracy versus tokens.
Parameter-count scaling, accuracy versus pretraining loss, and continuation-task scaling are untested. The token scaling uses checkpoints within a single cosine-schedule run, not separate runs.

missing.what: Qualitative comparison of scaling slopes (k values) across modalities: similar on sWUGGY except Speech-HuBERT; reduced by factors B and C on sBLIMP; affected by A, B and C on Topic-SC. The rows give no slope values or relative-slope information.

record.verdict_notes: The Figure 1 x-axis runs from 1e19 to 3e22 and is labelled 'trained tokens'. This is implausible given training sets of at most 7.7B tokens, so the axis is likely FLOPs-like compute or mislabelled. The 'scale' is checkpoints within one cosine-scheduled run of a single model size, a weaker test of V6 than separate runs. No numeric slopes or uncertainty are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds for speech or other modalities; the study compares modality performance but does not measure power-law loss.

Tests accuracy on three objective tasks against trained-token count during the first epoch. Does not test downstream performance against pretraining loss, continuation-task scaling, or parameter-count scaling.
Fitting-choice sensitivity, disagreement between published exponents, and curves bending away from a power law.

relationships.condition: All six modalities on sBLIMP and Topic-StoryCloze, and all except Speech-HuBERT on sWUGGY; 1.1B TinyLlama, checkpoints within the first epoch.
relationships.reason: The authors state that almost all straight lines fit well on log-log accuracy-vs-tokens axes, with positive slopes (R1–R5, R7–R18).
relationships.display_finding: Almost all tested accuracy-versus-token trajectories fit straight lines well on log-log axes with positive slopes.

relationships.reason: The text says this is the only non-positive slope, and converged accuracy is 50.8%, near chance (R6).
relationships.display_finding: The scaling slope was non-positive, and converged sWUGGY accuracy was 50.8%, near chance.

relationships.condition: Speech-HuBERT and Phone-Repeat on sBLIMP and Topic-StoryCloze.
relationships.reason: The text says factors B and C reduce scaling speed, so improvement with tokens is slower for speech-like tokens. This is based on the text; slopes are not given numerically (R11, R12, R17, R18).
relationships.display_finding: Speech-HuBERT and Phone-Repeat improved more slowly with training tokens on sBLIMP and Topic-StoryCloze because speech-like token properties reduced scaling speed.
